data.title: Tom Rust: Chief counsel and staff director, House Ethics Committee
data.description:
For nearly two decades, Tom Rust has worked behind the scenes to help police the conduct of lawmakers.

Rust joined the House Ethics Committee in 2009 after nearly a decade in private legal practice. He quickly moved up the ranks, serving as senior counsel and acting director of investigations before taking the role of staff director in 2014.

Today, Rust oversees roughly 30 staffers working across the committee’s advice, investigations and financial disclosure offices. He also advises the committee’s 10 members, who are evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

His work has included some of the House’s most high-profile ethics investigations.

Asked about the most interesting case he has encountered, Rust pointed to the investigation into former Rep. George Santos (R-N.Y.), whom the House voted to expel in 2023. Santos was sentenced to a seven-year prison term after he pleaded guilty to wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, but he was released from prison last year after President Trump commuted his sentence.

“There were just so many different issues there,” Rust said. “It was a wide-ranging case that involved allegations of criminal misconduct. It involved interactions with an ongoing criminal investigation. It was very high-profile.”

Rust said one of the most rewarding parts of his job is working with the committee members.

“If you took the transcript of our committee meeting and you took the names off the transcript, you oftentimes have trouble finding out which party somebody is in because our discussions are — they are very serious,” he said. “Our members all take it very seriously, and they are not particularly partisan in the room, which is great.”

That dynamic is also central to how Rust responds to accusations that the committee is partisan. Investigators frequently face criticism from the people they scrutinize, he said, but the committee’s evenly divided membership and nonpartisan staff provide an important safeguard.

“The best way to address any criticism of your work is just let your work speak for itself and do the best work possible,” Rust said.

The biggest challenge, he added, is the committee’s confidentiality. Because much of its work happens behind closed doors, outsiders can sometimes misunderstand its process.

For Rust, the mission remains the draw. He expects to remain with the committee for at least the next few years.

 He said protecting the integrity of the House is “a valuable thing.”

data.title: The latest court ruling against deportations ignores precedent and won't hold up
data.description:
A federal judge has declared two provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act unconstitutional in a ninety-page opinion that never mentions the Supreme Court cases upholding exactly such a law.

Recently, in Stanford Daily v. Rubio, Judge Noël Wise of the Northern District of California held that the government may not deport foreign visitors or revoke their visas based on “protected speech.” She declared the law’s foreign-policy removal and visa-revocation provisions unconstitutional to that extent.

Her opinion holds that noncitizens enjoy First Amendment rights to the same extent as citizens. For that proposition, it leans on the Ninth Circuit’s 1995 decision in American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee v. Reno. That case arose from the government’s effort to deport members and supporters of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.

Here is what Wise’s opinion leaves out: That very litigation all the way to the Supreme Court, where the ruling she cited was overturned. The government won the case.

In Reno v. American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, the Supreme Court held that Congress had stripped the lower courts of jurisdiction over such claims. Justice Antonin Scalia wrote for the court that “[a]s a general matter,” an alien “unlawfully in this country has no constitutional right to assert selective enforcement as a defense against his deportation,” and that the executive “should not have to disclose its ‘real’ reasons” for deporting particular foreign nationals.

The plaintiffs in this new case are lawfully present, so a careful court might have distinguished the case on that ground. But Wise did not do so. Her opinion cites the Ninth Circuit decision four times and completely omits the Supreme Court’s last word in the same case.

The Supreme Court’s ruling is part of a much larger jurisprudential pattern. In 1904, Turner v. Williams upheld the exclusion of an English anarchist for his advocacy. Chief Justice Melville Fuller wrote that governments “cannot be denied the power of self-preservation.” Wise failed to cite or acknowledge this case.

In Harisiades v. Shaughnessy, which might be the closest case to the current one, the Supreme Court in 1952 upheld the deportation of lawful permanent residents, one of whom had been in the country for thirty-eight years, due to Communist Party membership. The same First Amendment objection was rejected.

In Mathews v. Diaz, the Supreme Court in 1976 explained that in immigration, “Congress regularly makes rules that would be unacceptable if applied to citizens.” Wise failed even to cite this case, let alone confront its reasoning.

Another more recent case missing from Wise’s opinion is Trump v. Hawaii, which in 2018 upheld a statute allowing presidents to bar aliens they find “detrimental to the interests of the United States.” The court’s opinion states that the law “exudes deference to the president in every clause.”

Wise also fails to mention or confront or name the doctrine — “plenary power” — that has governed this area of law since the nineteenth century.

Contrary to what some say, foreigners lawfully among us do indeed have free-speech rights. The Supreme Court said as much in its 1945 decision in Bridges v. Wixon. However — and this is very important — removal from the U.S. is not a punishment.

In the Reno case mentioned above, the Supreme Court explained that a deported alien “is not being punished” for his conduct but “is merely being held to the terms under which he was admitted.” The court located the limit in the nature of the removal power rather than in any discount on the alien’s rights. A visa is an invitation, and this country’s invitations have always come with the understanding that the host, not the guest, decides when the arrangement has soured.

Nor did the host act on a whim. The referral letters and determination memoranda quoted in the opinion gave two reasons for the government’s actions. One was conduct “creating a hostile environment for Jewish students,” and the other was conduct “indicating support for a designated terrorist organization.”

Judge Wise recites both but weighs neither. Congress wrote the second reason into the statute books: Any alien who “endorses or espouses terrorist activity” is inadmissible and, under a companion provision, deportable. Yet Judge Wise, hunting for gentler alternatives to the provision she struck, oddly cites the statutory language as “speech-neutral.”

Yet the Supreme Court, for its part, held in 2010, in Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project, that Congress may imprison even American citizens if they engage in advocacy coordinated with designated terrorist groups. Under Wise’s ruling, the same government may not so much as un-invite a foreign guest who applauds a terrorist group’s massacres. The hierarchy is clearly upside down.

Wise declared the deportation provision unconstitutionally vague because it turns on the Secretary of State’s personal determination that a foreigner’s presence compromises “a compelling United States foreign policy interest.” Her supporting authorities are two district-court decisions: One that was reversed by the Third Circuit in 1996, the other which was vacated by that court this year. It’s not that Wise is unaware of this: Her opinion merely nods to both outcomes in a footnote and then marches on.

Meanwhile, Matter of Ruiz-Massieu, the 1996 Board of Immigration Appeals decision squarely upholding this provision against the same challenges, is acknowledged only as an example of enforcement history — its holding is never engaged. Judge Wise also quotes Secretary Rubio’s assurance that nobody loses a visa for protesting paper straws as proof that no standard exists. But a standard that separates paper straws from Hamas is not standardless. Most Americans could administer such a thing in their sleep, which may be why Congress assigned it to a cabinet officer rather than a faculty lounge.

There was an off-ramp for Wise, but she drove past it. Under Rust v. Sullivan and Justice Brandeis’s canonical rules in Ashwander v. TVA, a court facing constitutional doubts must first look for a saving construction. Yet “constitutional avoidance” appears nowhere in Wise’s opinion. Invalidating an act of Congress, even in part, is supposed to be a last resort, but Wise never even bothered to try another route.

Wise’s ruling is already being paraded by activists as vindication for Mahmoud Khalil — not least by Khalil himself. But it is nothing of the sort. It removes no one from proceedings, releases no one, vacates no removal order, and cancels no visa revocation. It also binds no other court. A district court opinion is precedent for nobody. Khalil, the Columbia graduate and green-card holder whose March 2025 arrest opened this drama, is not a party to the case, so the decision does not touch the order governing him.

Last September, an immigration judge ordered him removed on a separate ground: willful omissions from his green-card application, including his service with the United Nations Relief and Works Agency and his work in the Syria office of the British Embassy in Beirut. No ruling about protected speech can launder a false application.

The Stanford Daily has been here before. In the 1970s, after police searched its newsroom, the paper won a case in the district court and the Ninth Circuit, only to be reversed by the Supreme Court in Zurcher v. Stanford Daily. Every journalism student reads that case with a shudder. The Justice Department has sixty days to notice an appeal, but it shouldn’t take nearly that long to make its decision.

The Ninth Circuit should reverse Wise’s unwise ruling. If it prefers its own 1995 opinion to the way the Supreme Court ended that case in 1999, it can take its chances and remind everyone how that last Stanford Daily experiment ended.

The guest list of the U.S. belongs to its hosts. It is time the courts handed it back.

Mark Goldfeder is a former law professor and director of the National Jewish Advocacy Center.

data.title: Kamela White: Democratic clerk, Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Homeland Security
data.description:
Kamela White sees that numbers can tell a story — or be used to hide one.

As a clerk for Democrats on the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Homeland Security, White plays a role in shaping federal policy through government funding.

She said her biggest goal under the Trump administration has been to work for accountability as the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has been given unprecedented levels of funding with few strings attached.

White, 51, noted that the DHS has gotten more than a trillion dollars in federal funding amid “the evisceration of any sort of oversight.”

Some of that shifted, however, with the adoption of the 2026 budget more than a year into President Trump’s term and as GOP senators found they were also getting silence on their requests to the administration.

“I think a lot of the lack of information sharing, the lack of answering questions, it wasn’t just our questions; they weren’t answering the majority’s questions either. So there’s a shared frustration with the inability to get information that I think really helped us to have a lot of common ground,” she said.

“Otherwise, we’re just like, ‘What’d you spend that $190 billion on?’ Because they didn’t have to report a penny of it.”

White spent years at the Office of Management and Budget and served at U.S. Customs and Border Protection. She made the switch during former President Obama’s era after helping build out predictive analytics data to assess what personnel levels would be needed to respond to expected flows along the border and at ports of entry, shifting how Congress decided to fund the agency.

“What changed was you weren’t arguing over the numbers anymore,” she said, prompting the agency to realize it hadn’t been “telling our story.”

“You have a better opportunity to build that common ground if you’re able to introduce trusted data.”

Under Trump, White has also been part of the team investigating how immigration funding has been spent, uncovering that the DHS bought 12 planes without authorization for the purchases from Congress and paid above market rate for warehouses officials planned to turn into detention centers.

“By default, you are setting policy with funding,” she said, noting that some funding has strict parameters around its use.

She also said the committee’s Democrats were able to “restore some of the changes the administration put in place, and make it harder for them to either stonewall or not respond” to oversight.

“No oversight on money is a dangerous thing,” she said.

data.title: Wyndee Parker: National security adviser, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY)
data.description:
No two days are the same for Wyndee Parker.

As national security adviser to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), Parker is responsible for overseeing the activities of all of the lower chamber’s national security committees, including Armed Services, Intelligence, Foreign Affairs, Homeland Security and their Appropriations counterparts.

She also works with the executive branch and its corresponding agencies that make up the entire intelligence community, including the CIA, National Security Agency, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Defense Department, State Department and some elements of the Department of Homeland Security.

Day to day, she helps ensure information is flowing to Congress and lawmakers and their staff are “kept as informed as they should be about all of the executive branch activities, operations, etc.,” often working with the National Security Council to ensure that the right briefings come together.

On top of that, Parker ensures Jeffries is prepared for “a lot” of meetings with foreign dignitaries and senior executive branch officials, and she helps work on and review legislation that moves out of committees and onto the House floor, such as the National Defense Authorization Act — one of the largest bills Congress passes annually.

The role is a study in multitasking.

“No day is like any other,” she said.

Parker admits she was “a little skeptical” when she came to Capitol Hill 25 years ago to serve as counsel on the House Intelligence Committee. That was a few years after receiving her law degree from Ohio State University and working in the office of general counsels for both the CIA and FBI. 

“My supervisor at the time told me ‘you know, no day is like any other day that’s gone before.’ … A couple decades later, I’m saying the same thing said to me,” she said, attributing it to the nature of national security work. 

“The world is so dynamic. It keeps us definitely motivated and kind of energized,” Parker said before adding that the phone rings “too often, I should say, between the hours of midnight and 6 a.m.”

Prior to working for Jeffries, Parker was with another senior member of the Democratic Party for nearly 15 years: former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (Calif.), also serving as her national security adviser.

When she’s not up to her neck in national security matters, Parker said she relishes spending time with her husband and two children. 

“I cherish those moments,” she said.

data.title: Rubi Flores: Policy director, Congressional Hispanic Caucus
data.description:
Rubi Flores, 30, is a concert pianist turned policy director who has landed at the Congressional Hispanic Caucus (CHC) as it positions itself to fight the Trump administration on its mass deportation agenda and other issues key to Latinos.

An immigrant from Mexico who moved to the U.S. at age 10, Flores excelled not only at piano but at cello as well and aimed to make music her career. But as she advanced to college, some of the most competitive conservatories remained out of reach financially.

“It was one of the first times that the world told me no, and that made me evaluate, what are the circumstances to led me to not be able to have that dream?” she told The Hill. That question led to “opening up a lot of conversations in my mind of the inequities worldwide.”

“Undergrad, leadership positions, and things like this really make you think that, ‘Oh, I can change the world.’ And I wanted to change the world; I wanted to make it a little bit better,” she said.

College was also where Flores began to first engage in activism, and she set about achieving new dreams.

After a stint as a Fulbright scholar in Mexico, Flores interned at Fwd.us, where she tracked asylum policy across the globe. From there, she went to work on the Biden campaign as chief of staff to campaign manager Julie Chávez.

Now at the CHC, Flores said the group is evaluating how to best play to its strengths while in the minority, a role that has involved being an active voice in pushing back on President Trump’s immigration agenda, visiting detention centers and highlighting conditions, and filing amicus briefs in a bevy of litigation now before the courts.

Flores said being both an immigrant and a trans woman are crucial lenses for how she approaches her work, including how the party can protect both groups in an age where a larger share of Latinos than ever before backed the GOP when they voted for Trump.

On both issues, Flores said, “That’s my overall goal to make sure that we have positions that are winnable while staying true to our values and our efforts,” adding that programming for the caucus has discussed how to “inoculate themselves from a lot of attacks on from the right, and also how to just have an agenda that, while remaining popular, can defend the community.”

data.title: Nancy Mace calls for public execution of Lindsay Clancy
data.description:
Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) said Monday that Lindsay Clancy should be publicly executed, as the Massachusetts woman faces a new trial for allegedly murdering her three children.

“Her children are dead, she should be dead too,” Mace told TMZ.

The South Carolina Republican later said, “She should get the death penalty. It should be public, it should be a public execution,” adding Clancy “deserves nothing less” than such a punishment.

“It could be by firearm, it could electric chair, I don’t really care,” the outgoing lawmaker added, later saying it would serve as a “warning to women everywhere [that] you don’t kill your kids.”

Judge William Sullivan, who is overseeing the case, declared a mistrial earlier this month. That came after the jury, composed of nine women and three men, told him they were unable to come to a unanimous decision after seven days of deliberation and five weeks of testimony.

Prior to Sullivan declaring a mistrial, the jurors said they had an 11-1 majority in favor of acquittal by reason of insanity due to postpartum psychosis, with one holdout.

Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz (R) has not said whether he will retry the case. A court hearing on the case is scheduled for Sept. 29 at Plymouth Superior Court, with Clancy being held at a psychiatric facility until then.

Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, has asked President Trump for a pardon — despite the president not having the authority to do so, as Clancy is facing state, and not federal, charges. 

After Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4, Trump called the situation “a horrible tragedy.”

The president told reporters, “Look, [Clancy] did a horrible, horrible thing. Can’t be worse, but you’ll find out what the price to pay is. There’ll be a price. It’s going to be [a] mental institution or jail or something, but I guess they’re going to go through another trial. It’s too bad.”

data.title: Russia sanctions bill passes House Rules Committee
data.description:
The House Rules Committee on Monday approved bipartisan legislation aimed at increasing sanctions on Russia amid its war in Ukraine.

The bill, which the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) championed, would allow President Trump to impose penalties on individuals working on behalf of the Russian government to stall peace negotiations with Ukraine, violate a negotiated peace agreement and subvert the Ukrainian government. 

The bill would allow Trump to impose visa- and property-blocking sanctions on Russian President Vladimir Putin, certain Russian military commanders and “any foreign person that knowingly provides defense items” to the Russian military.

Under the legislation, Trump would also be able to increase the tariff rate to 500 percent on goods from Russia and countries “that knowingly engage in the exchange of Russian-origin uranium and petroleum products.”

The House rules panel passing the measure likely sets up a full floor vote on the bill for later this week, as multiple outlets have reported. The Senate passed the bill via an 86-11 vote last month.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said it was “great news” that the House will reportedly vote on the “much-needed” legislation.

“Ukrainian civilians continue to be killed by Putin’s war machine, and this bill hits the Kremlin’s coffers hard. Now is the time to pass it and force Putin to the negotiating table,” Shaheen said Friday in a statement.

The House is set to depart on a seven-week recess at the close of business Thursday. But Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told reporters Monday he could fast-track the Russia sanctions bill via a process that would require a two-thirds majority, Politico reported. 

July marked the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022, according to the United Nations. Trump has enlisted his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and special envoy Steve Witkoff to broker a peace deal between Russian and Ukrainian officials to no avail.

data.title: Blanche to hold press briefing in Rose Garden Tuesday
data.description:
Attorney General Todd Blanche will brief reporters in the White House Rose Garden on Tuesday, as he will become the latest administration official to fill the shoes of former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt.

A White House official confirmed to NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network, that Blanche will speak to members of the press. 

Blanche joined Vice President Vance in Missouri on Monday to announce federal action taken against those suspected of stealing millions from taxpayers via a COVID-19 era small business relief program.

That came 11 days after Vance spoke to reporters inside the White House press briefing room, the first such briefing since July and the first since Leavitt departed the administration at the end of last month.

Leavitt’s departure sparked a search for a new press secretary, with Trump telling reporters on Sunday he “may have” developed a short list of candidates.

“We have a lot of people that want it,” the president said during a trip to Ireland. 

Trump also said Secretary of State Marco Rubio was “next” to brief reporters, mentioning Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Education Secretary Linda McMahon as possible future briefers.

During Leavitt’s maternity leave earlier this year, Vance, Rubio and Bessent briefed reporters in her absence. 

Blanche, whom the Senate confirmed to the full-time attorney general post last month, told CBS News on Monday the federal government will continue releasing records related to the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

“The one thing that we are not doing, we’re not protecting people,” Blanche said. “The reason that we’re not releasing documents has nothing to do with protecting any government or any entity. It’s just to protect, genuine classified [information].”

Family members of Sept. 11 victims have criticized the administration for allegedly shielding the Saudi Arabian government from scrutiny for its role in the attacks.

data.title: Supreme Court won't restore Trump's mail-in voting plan for midterms
data.description:
The Supreme Court refused to clear the way for President Trump’s mail-in voting plan for the midterms on Monday over the dissents of two conservative justices, keeping intact a judge’s block that declared the plan unlawful.

It’s the third time the Trump administration brought the plan to the high court’s emergency docket after groups have blocked the effort.  

Previously, the justices ruled in Trump’s favor, finding that blue states likely had no right to sue over the president’s executive order itself. Now, they’ve ruled against him in the latest phase, which focused on the U.S. Postal Service’s implementation of the president’s directive as Election Day rapidly approaches. 

“The Government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the District Court’s preliminary injunction,” the court’s brief, unsigned ruling reads. 

Justice Brett Kavanaugh, one of Trump’s appointees to the court, publicly indicated he voted with the majority. He said there’s at least a fair prospect that Trump’s plan is legal. 

“But applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections,” Kavanaugh wrote. 

Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito publicly dissented. 

“Some of the plaintiffs lack standing, while the remainder are pursuing a claim that this Court has recently called a ‘Hail Mary pass’ that ‘rarely succeeds,’” wrote Alito, joined by Thomas. 

No other justice publicly disclosed their vote. 

The plan would’ve required states to upload lists of voters to send them a mail ballot. The Postal Service would also only deliver ballots that meet new design requirements, like an official logo and barcode. 

It became the latest emergency case to thrust the justices into the midterm elections. The Supreme Court last week lifted an order instructing Missouri they could use Republicans’ newly passed congressional map. And, the justices are still mulling yet another case, which concerns the use of an overhauled immigration clearinghouse to scrutinize voter rolls. 

It also marks a rare loss for the president on the  high court’s emergency docket. Though it hasn’t been a clean sweep, the justices have repeatedly agreed to step in after judges have blocked key aspects of Trump’s agenda. 

The mail-in voting lawsuits began after Trump signed a new executive order in March targeting the practice, which he continually claims contributes to significant fraud. Election officials have identified limited instances of fraud, but no evidence has emerged suggesting the massive scale Trump has described. 

The lawsuits claim the plan exceeds Trump’s authority. 

Blue states had warned of chaos under the administration’s plan, saying that it would be impossible to comply ahead of November’s contests. Some had suggested it would leave millions unable to vote by mail.  

“The efforts that state and local elections officials would have to undertake to even begin an attempt at compliance are herculean,” the states wrote in court filings last week. 

Solicitor General D. John Sauer has described the plan as modest, emphasizing that federal immigration authorities aren’t second-guessing states’ mail voter lists. He argued it was well within USPS’s authority to regulate how to handle sensitive mail and called the judge’s block “baseless.” 

“Every day that the district court’s injunction remains in place, more ballots are being sent through the U.S. Mail without the benefits that the Rule provides for election integrity,” Sauer wrote in court filings last week. 

The case has come to the Supreme Court’s emergency docket three times, each after U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani issued a block stopping the president. She is an appointee of former President Obama who serves on the federal trial bench in Boston. 

In the first round, which focused on Trump’s original executive order itself from the spring, the Supreme Court said the blue states suing likely had no right to sue over it. 

In August, the Postal Service announced its final plan to implement the president’s directive for the midterms. 

When Talwani temporary halted that, too, the Justice Department brought the case back to the high court. But before the justices ruled, Talwani replaced her block with a new, longer one. Then, the administration filed a third and latest plea at the Supreme Court. 

As the Supreme Court keeps Talwani’s block in place, U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, a Trump appointee who serves in the nation’s capital, blocked Trump’s policy nationwide on Sunday in response to separate challenges. That ruling had not yet reached the justices.

data.title: Paxton gets $54M boost from Senate Leadership Fund's Texas PAC
data.description:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s (R) Senate campaign received nearly $54 million from the GOP-aligned Senate Leadership Fund’s (SLF) Texas affiliate, according to a filing.

The Austin-based Texas PAC donated more than $53.8 million to Paxton’s campaign, based on filings to the Federal Election Commission (FEC). The committee is affiliated with the SLF, which is tied to Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.).

Texas PAC also purchased more than $51 million worth of ad reservations on Friday, per media tracking firm AdImpact. The ads will air in the Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, San Antonio and Austin media markets, the Texas Tribune reported Friday.

Paxton’s campaign was at a significant financial disadvantage earlier this summer to that of his opponent, state Rep. James Talarico (D). As of the end of June, Talarico’s campaign had more than $21.5 million on hand to less than $1.8 million for Paxton, according to FEC data.

But outside GOP groups have sought to close the gap. The National Republican Senatorial Committee, which attacked Paxton for alleged infidelity during his primary race against Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), set up a joint fundraising committee with the Texas attorney general’s campaign in June.

Then earlier this month, President Trump’s MAGA Inc. Super PAC paid $10 million to Del Ray Media, which released two attack ads against Talarico.

The Hill has reached out to spokespeople for the Paxton and Talarico campaigns for comment on the SLF’s spending in the race.

Talarico is trying to be the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas since former Sen. Lloyd Bentsen in 1988. The 37-year-old has campaigned on raising taxes on billionaires and corporations, while going after Paxton for his estranged wife, state Sen. Angela Paxton (R), accusing him of infidelity and the Texas House impeaching him in 2023. 

Paxton, meanwhile, has argued Talarico’s views are out of step with the majority of those in the Lone Star State. The state attorney general has specifically gone after Talarico’s views on culture war issues, such as his support for transgender children. 

As of Sunday, Decision Desk HQ gave Talarico a 55 percent chance of winning the race. The Democratic nominee also led Paxton 48 percent to 44 percent in a recent AARP survey of likely Texas voters.

Talarico’s lead over Paxton in that poll was outside the margin of error of 3.3 percentage points, while 8 percent of respondents were undecided.
